chunks.text: Dispatch · June 14, twenty twenty-six · 9 min read · By Don Goldstein

On June 10, the Bureau of Labor Statistics published the May Consumer Price Index. Restaurant menu prices rose 3.5% over the year; groceries rose 2.7%. Underneath that gap is one ingredient doing most of the work, and one doing the opposite. Here is the read for an operator pricing a summer menu.
In short

Over the twelve months to May twenty twenty-six, restaurant menu prices (food away from home) rose 3.5% while grocery prices (food at home) rose 2.7%, the menu line is moving faster than the grocery aisle.
Beef is the driver: Usda's May forecast puts twenty twenty-six beef-and-veal prices up 12.1%, the biggest mover on the board, on a cattle herd that has been shrinking since twenty nineteen.
Eggs are the relief: the same forecast has egg prices down 29.8% for the year as the flock recovers from avian flu, the one line on your invoice headed the other way.
A national forecast is not your invoice. Muntin's own Cost Index has wholesale ribeye flagged flat this week even with the yearly trend up, the argument for pricing off your actual vendor prices.
The summer move: find the two or three plates where beef carries the cost, run the plate math on this week's number, and decide raise, re-engineer, or hold one plate at a time.
Are restaurant prices rising faster than groceries in twenty twenty-six?

Yes, over the twelve months to May twenty twenty-six, restaurant prices rose 3.5% while groceries rose 2.7% (Bls Consumer Price Index), so menus are now outrunning the grocery aisle. The number that matters for a restaurant printed on June 10. Over the twelve months ending in May twenty twenty-six, the food-away-from-home index, the Bureau of Labor Statistics’ name for restaurant, cafeteria, and vending meals, rose 3.5%. The food-at-home index, what a household pays at the grocery store, rose 2.7%. The menu line is now moving faster than the grocery aisle, and your guest feels both.

That gap sets the frame a diner brings to your check. When groceries climb faster than menus, eating out reads as the relative bargain. When menus climb faster, where we are now, the comparison runs the other way and a price bump lands harder. The 3.5% is not a number you can pass along without thinking about the 2.7% your guest is also living, and use that gap while it lasts, because Usda’s full-year forecast has the two lines converging by fall.

A bar chart of twelve-month price changes through May twenty twenty-six, from the May Consumer Price Index, drawn to scale. Restaurant menus, the food-away-from-home index, rose three point five percent. The all-food index rose three point one percent. Grocery prices, the food-at-home index, rose two point seven percent, the lowest of the three. Restaurant menus are rising faster than the grocery aisle.
Beef is the driver. Eggs are the relief.

The 3.5% is an average, and averages hide the plates that actually hurt. When the Usda’s Economic Research Service refreshed its Food Price Outlook in May, it did not only nudge the all-food forecast up to 3.4% for twenty twenty-six. It named the culprit. Beef and veal are forecast to rise 12.1% this year, the single biggest mover on the board, with a forecast range that runs as high as 18%. The cause is structural, not a blip: the U.S. cattle herd has been shrinking since twenty nineteen, supply is tight, and demand has held up anyway.

The same forecast carries the counter-story, the one line on your invoice headed the other way. Egg prices are forecast to fall 29.8% in twenty twenty-six as the laying flock recovers from the avian-flu outbreak that pushed a dozen past six dollars last year. If your menu leans on eggs, brunch, baking, a heavy hand of aioli, the math is finally working in your favor while the beef plates work against you.

Usda's twenty twenty-six retail price forecasts by food category, from the May Food Price Outlook. Beef and veal are forecast up twelve point one percent, the largest increase on the chart. Fresh vegetables up seven point eight percent. Sugar and sweets up six point three percent. Nonalcoholic beverages, which include coffee, up five point eight percent. Pork up one point five percent. Poultry up half a percent. Eggs are forecast down twenty-nine point eight percent, the only category falling and the single biggest move on the chart.
The headline is not your invoice.

Here is the gap, from our own data. As of June 5, Muntin’s Cost Index had wholesale ribeye near 11.59 dollars a pound, up sharply across the last two years, but flagged flat for the week, sitting inside its normal range. The annual forecast says beef is up 12.1%. Both are true, and only one of them is on your invoice this Tuesday.

That is the difference between a forecast and a feed. A 12.1% annual number does not mean your ribeye costs 12.1% more this week than last; it means the year, averaged out, is expected to land there. The week-to-week reality is bumpier, and it is local. Re-price your ribeye plate off the headline the morning it prints, and you have moved against a cost that, this week, had not.

That is the whole argument for reading your invoices instead of the news. The forecast tells you which way to lean over the season. Your vendor’s last three invoices tell you whether to move this week. Muntin Ledger exists for that second job: it reads each invoice as it lands and flags a line when it jumps against your own history, not against a national average.

How Muntin Ledger flags a price increase against your own purchase history, in four steps. One, drop the invoice: a photo or P D F lands in the inbox and the line items are read and filed. Two, match to your history: each line is matched to what you paid that same vendor before. Three, compare against your own baseline: the check is against your last invoices for that item, not a national index. Four, flag the move: if a price has jumped beyond its normal range, the line is flagged so you decide before the plate quietly loses margin.
The plate math, on this week’s number.

Let me walk it the way I would on a slow Tuesday at the host stand at Tacombi, with the caveat up front: the plate below is an illustrative worked example, not a specific menu item, and the only hard number in it is the ribeye price from the Cost Index. Everything else is round numbers chosen to make the math legible.

Say a ribeye runs about 11.59 dollars a pound wholesale this week. An eight-ounce finished portion is half a pound of meat on the plate, so call it 5.80 dollars in protein before you account for the trim and fat you cut away, and trim is real, so the true figure is higher. For the example, say sides, sauce, and garnish add another 3.20 dollars, putting the plate’s food cost near 9.00 dollars. On an illustrative 30 dollars menu price, that is a 30% food cost, roughly where a full-service plate wants to sit. The skeleton, for your own plate: portion in pounds times your price per pound, plus the sides, divided by the menu price, is your food-cost percentage.

Now run the forecast through it as a season-end sanity check, not a reason to re-price this week. If beef lands where Usda expects for the year, 12.1% on that 5.80 dollars of protein is about 6.50 dollars, and the plate’s food cost crosses 31%, then 32%. None of those crossings is a crisis on its own. Stacked across every beef plate on the menu, over a year, they are the difference between a printed margin and a real one. The point of the math is not the single plate; it is catching the drift before it has happened to forty covers a night for six months.
Your beef line jumped, raise, re-engineer, or hold?

When the Ledger flags a beef line, or your own eye catches it on the invoice, you have three honest moves and one reflex to avoid. The reflex is to raise every price a little to cover it. That is the move that loses the guest who was already doing the menu-versus-grocery math from the top of this piece. The better path is plate by plate.

A decision tree for one beef plate after a confirmed cost increase, in four checks. Check one: is this plate a signature people come for? If yes, hold the price, protect the draw, and make the margin back elsewhere. If no, go to check two. Check two: can the plate be re-engineered without the guest feeling it, through portion, trim, a blended cut, or a cheaper supporting ingredient? If yes, re-engineer and recost it, keeping the price. If no, go to check three. Check three: is the plate priced below its category on your own menu? If yes, raise this one plate to its category, a single targeted move. If no, the warning: do not reach for a board-wide price bump to cover one ingredient.
The honest take.

Two things are true at once, and a piece pegged to a single data release should say both. The first: over the last twelve months, restaurant prices did rise faster than groceries, 3.5% against 2.7%, and beef is most of the reason. The second, quieter one: Usda’s full-year twenty twenty-six forecast actually has the two lines converging, groceries up 3.2%, restaurants up 3.5%, because the grocery aisle is now catching up, led by the same beef and the same produce. The gap you can use to frame value this summer may be narrower by fall.

And a forecast is a forecast. Usda’s own range on beef runs from about 7% to 18%; the egg call could be off by ten points in either direction. These are the best public read available, and they are still a model fitted to recent data, not a promise. Treat the direction as solid, beef up, eggs down, restaurants and groceries both rising, and treat the decimal as provisional.

What is not provisional is your own paperwork. The national numbers tell you which way the season leans. Your last three invoices for each item tell you what to do this week. Price off the second one.
Frequently asked questions.

Are restaurant prices rising faster than grocery prices in twenty twenty-six? Over the twelve months ending May twenty twenty-six, yes: the food-away-from-home index rose 3.5% while food at home rose 2.7%, per the May Cpi. Usda’s full-year twenty twenty-six forecast has them closer, restaurants 3.5%, groceries 3.2%, as grocery prices catch up over the year.

Why is beef so expensive in twenty twenty-six? The U.S. cattle herd has been shrinking since twenty nineteen, so supply is tight while demand has stayed strong. Usda forecasts beef and veal prices up 12.1% for twenty twenty-six, the largest increase among food categories, with a forecast range of roughly 7% to 18%.

Are egg prices going down? Yes. After the avian-flu spike that pushed eggs past six dollars a dozen in early twenty twenty-five, the flock is recovering and Usda forecasts retail egg prices down about 29.8% for twenty twenty-six, the one major food category expected to fall this year.

How much have restaurant prices gone up in twenty twenty-six? Restaurant menu prices rose 3.5% over the twelve months ending May twenty twenty-six (Bls Cpi, food away from home), with full-service meals up 3.8% and limited-service up 3.3%. That is slower than the twenty twenty-two, 23 spike but still ahead of grocery inflation at 2.7%.

How do I work out a menu price from food cost? Divide the plate’s ingredient cost by your target food-cost percentage. A plate that costs about 9.00 dollars to make at a 30% target prices near 30 dollars. Run it on your actual vendor price this week, not a national average.

How much should I raise menu prices? Not board-wide to cover one ingredient. Find the plates where the rising item carries the cost, run the plate math on your actual vendor price, and move plate by plate, hold a signature, re-engineer where the guest will not feel it, raise a single plate priced under its category. Price off your invoices, not the headline.
Key takeaways
Find the two or three plates where beef carries the cost, that is where this lands first.
Run the plate math on your actual vendor price this week, not the 12.1% national headline.
Hold a signature plate, re-engineer where the guest will not notice, raise one plate priced under its category.
Skip the board-wide price bump, it taxes every guest for a problem that lives on a few plates.
Lean on the eggs-down, beef-up split now; Usda's full-year forecast has menus and groceries converging by fall.
